items.title: 52263_Sonny Greer oral history interview
items.q: He was over Dutch Schultz, Al Capone and all of them.

ctx.x: I've seen him. But my man was the top man. My man was a top man. He was over Dutch Schultz, Al Capone and all of them. He wasn't a -- a little, tiny guy. Talked like a girl. Never raised his voice. Owney Madden. Owney Madden. He owned the Cotton Club. When he said something, that was it. And he loved -- he loved Duke because him and Duke used to sit up and play "Grits" and all that, "Coon Can" all night long after the club closed. Me, I'm ready to run. When the last note hit, I'm gone. I say, I don't play that…

But he loved Duke and he loved me. And his influence was so powerful that we was always in the clear. He'd say, "Duke and Sonny are my boys." Guys, even I recall one time, first time we ever played the theater in Chicago, you know, I told you about that. So we come off the stage after the first show. I came off the stage, I'm the last one off the stage because the other guys just sat down. Taft But I was the last one because I had all the equipment, I had to check to see all that. I'd come off and I wanted to see…
